input: Write a due diligence memo on Databricks

red_flags.claim: Copyright exposure warrants closer diligence: the DBRX infringement claim survived dismissal. This establishes litigation exposure, not infringement or damages.

Customer cost control and onboarding complexity are diligence priorities: G2 reviewers repeatedly cite pricing complexity and a steep learning curve. These are user reports, not evidence of measured churn.

People-management watchpoint: Glassdoor's snapshot rates work-life balance at 3.3/5, below the overall 4.1/5 employee rating; recent reviews also mention politics and stalled progression. This is self-selected review evidence, not a workforce-wide finding.

traction.claim: Company claim, as of the announcement: more than 20,000 organizations worldwide, including 70% of the Fortune 500, use Databricks. Named customers include adidas, AT&T, Bayer, Block, Mastercard, Rivian and Unilever.
Company claim: more than 1,000 customers were consuming at an annualized revenue run-rate above $1 million each, including more than 100 above $10 million each.
Company claim on the undated page opened for this review: Databricks has more than 1,200 global cloud, independent-software-vendor and consulting partners.
Company claim, as of this announcement: net retention exceeded 140%. A newer retention figure was not verified in the opened pages.

missing_fields: Audited financial statements, recognized full-year revenue, GAAP net income and cash balance were not verified.
An official current employee total and confirmed layoff history were not verified; the workforce figures below measure observed professional profiles.
Final or current dispositions of the copyright and patent cases as of 2026-11-04 were not verified.
A definitive regulatory-enforcement record and authoritative sanctions-screening result were not verified; no clean-record conclusion is offered.
A confirmed breach scope or definitive later resolution of the TeamPCP allegation was not verified.
A longitudinal employee-review trend was not verified; only a review-platform snapshot and recent individual reviews were opened.
A complete financing-round history and the equity leads for the older Series J and Series L rounds were not verified from the opened closing announcements.

legal_and_regulatory.claim: In In re Mosaic LLM Litigation, No. 24-cv-01451-CRB, the Northern District of California denied dismissal of the direct copyright-infringement claim tied to DBRX and denied the motion to strike. The court found the allegations sufficient to proceed, not that infringement had occurred.
A subsequent order in the same copyright litigation established amicus-briefing procedures for summary-judgment motions. This was a procedural order, not a final merits disposition.

In R2 Solutions LLC v. Databricks, Inc., No. 4:23-cv-01147, the Eastern District of Texas granted motions striking certain Databricks supplemental invalidity contentions and expert opinions, while denying Databricks' competing strike and supplemental-claim-construction motions. These were procedural patent-case rulings, not a liability judgment.

SANS reported an alleged TeamPCP-linked compromise. Its March 30 update quoted Databricks saying it had thoroughly investigated its internal systems and 'found nothing'; the report did not establish a confirmed Databricks breach or customer-data impact.

reputation.claim: Glassdoor aggregator snapshot: 4.1/5 from 1,705 employee reviews, with 77% recommending the company and work-life balance at 3.3/5. Reviews dated October 20–21, 2026 praise technology, leadership and opportunities, while others mention politics and stalled career progression; no measured historical rating trend was verified.

G2 aggregator snapshot: 4.6/5 from 1,401 customer reviews. Reviews dated October 20–30, 2026 praise unified engineering, analytics and machine learning, collaboration and scale; recurring complaints concern learning curve and cost management, with individual reports of slow large queries and notebook Git friction.

Critical press: The Register covered authors' allegations that DBRX involved copyrighted books from pirated training material and Databricks' challenge to that account. The coverage concerned contested allegations and a surviving lawsuit, not an adjudicated infringement finding.

output.verdict: Databricks' reported enterprise adoption, rapid run-rate growth and financing access look strong, alongside technical founders and broadly positive customer reviews. Deeper diligence should validate audited economics and valuation, obtain current litigation, security and sanctions findings, and test consumption-cost controls and talent retention before an investment decision.

financial_signals.claim: Company claim: revenue run-rate exceeded $7 billion, with more than 80% year-over-year growth during its second quarter. This is an annualized run-rate statement, not verified recognized annual revenue.
Company claim: adjusted free cash flow was positive over the preceding twelve months. This does not establish GAAP net profitability.

Unify aggregator data: observed professional profiles increased 15.8%, from 12,299 in August 2025 to 14,237 in July 2026. These are profile-coverage counts, not company-reported employee totals, and may lag internal changes.
Unify recorded 2,822 observed hire events in its latest twelve-month event window. This is an aggregator hiring signal, not verified company gross hiring or net job creation.

team.claim: Databricks' own history identifies its 2013 founding team as Ali Ghodsi, Matei Zaharia, Ion Stoica, Patrick Wendell, Reynold Xin, Andy Konwinski and Arsalan Tavakoli-Shiraji, emerging from UC Berkeley's AMPLab work.
The current company leadership page lists Ali Ghodsi as co-founder and CEO, David Conte as CFO, Ron Gabrisko as chief revenue officer and Hatim Shafique as chief operating officer.
Matei Zaharia's university biography identifies him as Databricks co-founder and CTO and an associate professor at UC Berkeley.

Prior-company background: Databricks' CFO appointment announcement says Dave Conte previously served as CFO at Splunk and Opsware and began his career at Ernst & Young. His current CFO role is separately supported by the leadership page.

Notable announced transition within the review period: Bloomberg reported that AI head Naveen Rao planned to leave to launch a computer startup. Databricks confirmed a transition to an advisory role and plans to invest in the venture; the article did not provide an effective departure date.

business.claim: Databricks sells an enterprise Data + AI Platform built on an open lakehouse architecture, combining governed data with organization-specific AI capabilities for technical teams and broader business users.

The business model is consumption-based: the pricing page describes pay-as-you-go compute usage, billed at per-second granularity, with storage, networking and related costs varying by selected services and cloud provider.
Databricks is headquartered in San Francisco, has offices around the world and serves organizations worldwide. These geographic statements come from the company page opened for this review.

funding.claim: Latest completed financing verified: Databricks announced a $5 billion strategic equity round at a $190 billion valuation, led by Coatue, with Blackstone, MGX, T. Rowe Price-advised accounts and Sixth Street Growth among the investors.

Databricks said it was completing approximately $5 billion of Series L equity financing at a $134 billion valuation and approximately $2 billion of additional debt capacity. Named equity participants included JPMorganChase, Glade Brook Capital, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Microsoft and others; JPMorgan Chase led the credit facilities. Debt capacity is not necessarily drawn debt.

Databricks announced the final close of its $10 billion Series J at a $62 billion valuation and a separate $5.25 billion credit facility. Investors disclosed at this close included QIA, Temasek, Macquarie-administered entities and Meta; the opened closing notice did not identify the equity round lead.
